content: Pfiesteria piscicida is a type of dinoflagellate that some researchers have attributed to numerous harmful algal blooms along the North Carolina coast during the 1980s and 1990s. The organism is named after Lois Ann Pfiester (1936–1992), a scientist who studied dinoflagellates. Its species name, piscicida, translates to fish-killer. Pfiesteria was first identified by JoAnn Burkholder at North Carolina State University. A detailed account of her discovery is documented in the book And the Waters Turned to Blood by Rodney Barker. Life Cycle Research on the life cycle of Pfiesteria has yielded conflicting results. Some peer-reviewed studies by government and university experts have described its life cycle as highly complex, involving at least 24 distinct stages, ranging from cyst forms to various amoeboid forms. However, other peer-reviewed studies have reported a much simpler life cycle, with no evidence of a toxic amoebic stage. The initial research suggested that the organism could transition through multiple stages depending on environmental conditions. In contrast, findings from 2002 indicate that the life cycle is far less intricate than previously believed and that the true Pfiesteria organism is non-toxic. Toxicity Advanced DNA analyses have revealed that Pfiesteria lacks the genetic structures necessary to produce the toxic proteins typically associated with harmful dinoflagellates. However, other researchers have successfully isolated and characterized a toxin from Pfiesteria piscicida, identifying the mechanisms by which the organism transitions from a non-toxic to a toxic state. These findings were published in the peer-reviewed journal Environmental Science and Technology on January 11, 2007. Human Health Research on the effects of Pfiesteria toxins on human health remains limited. At a multi-state workshop held by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in Atlanta, Georgia, in September 1997, attendees identified clinical symptoms associated with exposure to Pfiesteria toxins. These symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal cramps. Surveillance data suggest that Pfiesteria-related illnesses can be better tracked when lesions are observed in at least 20% of a 50-fish sample of the same species. Pfiesteria toxins have been implicated in adverse health effects among individuals who have had close contact with waters where the organism is abundant. Since June 1997, the Maryland Department of Health and Hygiene has been collecting data from physicians across the state on illnesses suspected to be caused by Pfiesteria toxins. By late October 1997, 146 individuals reported illnesses after exposure to diseased fish or waters suspected of Pfiesteria activity. Many of these individuals were watermen or commercial fishermen. The strongest evidence of adverse human health effects comes from case studies of two research scientists who were exposed to Pfiesteria in their North Carolina laboratory in 1993. Both scientists reported persistent cognitive impairments, particularly after physical exertion. Experiments conducted by researchers at Duke University Medical Center on rats demonstrated that the toxin appeared to slow learning processes but did not affect memory.
